t:
(a) If it has been finally determined by a court or Federal agency that any person intentionally affixed a label bearing a “Made in America” inscription, or any inscription with the same meaning, to any product sold in or shipped to the United States that is not made in the United States, the person shall be ineligible to receive any contract or subcontract made with funds made available in this Act, pursuant to the debarment, suspension, and ineligibility procedures described in sections 9.400 through 9.409 of title 48, Code of Federal Regulations. 
    (b)
        (1) To the extent practicable, with respect to authorized purchases of promotional items, funds made available by this Act shall be used to purchase items that are manufactured, produced, or assembled in the United States, its territories, or its possessions. 
        (2) The term “promotional items” has the meaning given the term in OMB Circular A–87, Attachment B, Item (1)(f)(3).

fable.w: The tempting reading is that the reference to a determination "by a court or Federal agency" and to debarment procedures implies outside-party involvement in a federal decision. It does not: the section only imposes contract ineligibility on persons found to have used false "Made in America" labels and directs that promotional items be bought domestically. It creates no comment period, hearing, advisory body, consultation with outside entities, new rulemaking authority, or right to sue. An enforcement or adjudicatory consequence against a person is not participation in a policy decision.
fable.s: the person shall be ineligible to receive any contract or subcontract made with funds made available in this Act, pursuant to the debarment, suspension, and ineligibility procedures

qwen_block.w: This section establishes penalties (ineligibility for contracts) for mislabeling products and sets procurement preferences for domestic goods. It does not require the federal government to consult with or coordinate with outside parties before making a decision. The reference to 'debarment, suspension, and ineligibility procedures' refers to existing regulatory processes for enforcing contract rules, not a new participation mechanism like a public hearing or advisory committee. The definition explicitly excludes applications for contracts or licenses.
qwen_block.s: the person shall be ineligible to receive any contract or subcontract made with funds made available in this Act, pursuant to the debarment, suspension, and ineligibility procedures described in sections 9.400 through 9.409 of title 48, Code of Federal Regulations.

opus.w: The section makes people who mislabel products as 'Made in America' ineligible for federal contracts and sets a buy-American preference for promotional items. Nothing in it requires consulting outsiders, holding public hearings, taking public comment, or setting up an advisory body before a federal decision. The reference to debarment procedures could look like participation, but any chance to respond is an individual defense against an enforcement finding (like Example 11), and contract eligibility is explicitly excluded.
opus.s: the person shall be ineligible to receive any contract or subcontract made with funds made available in this Act, pursuant to the debarment, suspension, and ineligibility procedures described in sections 9.400 through 9.409 of title 48, Code of Federal Regulations
opus.b: The tempting reading is "Yes," because subsection (a) brings in the FAR debarment and suspension procedures, which give the contractor notice and a chance to respond. That fails the definition for two reasons. First, the contractor responding to a charge against itself is like the manufacturer in Example 11: it is answering an enforcement finding, not taking part in a policy decision. Second, the provision is about whether someone can receive federal contracts, and contract eligibility is one of the listed exclusions. Subsection (b) only sets a buy-American preference for promotional items.

qwen_chat.w: This section establishes eligibility criteria for contractors and procurement preferences for the federal government. It does not require the government to consult with outside parties, hold public hearings, or form advisory committees with non-federal members before making decisions. The debarment is a penalty based on a prior final determination, and the purchase requirement is an internal directive for spending funds, not a participatory process involving outsiders in the decision.
qwen_chat.s: (a) If it has been finally determined by a court or Federal agency that any person intentionally affixed a label bearing a “Made in America” inscription... the person shall be ineligible to receive any contract... (b) To the extent practicable... funds made available by this Act shall be used to purchase items that are manufactured, produced, or assembled in the United States...
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the requirement to purchase items "manufactured... in the United States" involves coordination with domestic manufacturers or that the debarment process involves a hearing. However, the text describes procurement preferences and eligibility criteria for contractors, not a process where outside parties participate in the government's decision-making. The debarment is a consequence of a prior final determination, and the purchase requirement is a directive to the agency, not a consultation with outsiders.
